I am an economist and PhD candidate in the Department of Economics, Faculty of
Economics and Business, Universitas Indonesia, and a civil servant in the
Provincial Government of North Sulawesi. My work has two strands that are
usually kept apart: empirical research on how communities absorb large physical
shocks, and professional practice in Indonesian public procurement. They share a
single question: how public resources and collective capacity are actually
allocated when institutions are under strain.

My dissertation, *Shaking Land and Shaking Lives: Essays on the Economic Impacts
of Seismic Disasters*, is supervised by M. Halley Yudhistira and due for
completion in early 2028. The first chapter combines twenty years of Indonesia's
Village Potential Survey with village-level earthquake intensity surfaces and
finds a pattern that neither of the standard stories predicts: reported communal
conflict falls after damage-level shaking, while theft rises sharply on the same
villages in the same waves. Not a general improvement in security, then, but a
change in the *kind* of violence a community can produce. That chapter is
supported by a research grant from the ReCIPE Programme, funded by the Centre
for Economic Policy Research and the UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development
Office. The second chapter turns to what households pay for religious and
ceremonial activity after a shock, using expenditure rather than stated belief
to test whether religion functions as informal insurance.

Building these papers has meant building the data infrastructure they rest on:
harmonising two decades of village boundary change onto a constant reference
year, converting seismic intensity rasters into village-level exposure, and
documenting the whole chain so that it can be reproduced. That work is
unglamorous and, in the Indonesian context, largely unavailable off the shelf.
It is also where most of the credibility of the results comes from. Alongside
the research I work as a teaching assistant in the graduate econometrics
sequence at Universitas Indonesia, across the doctoral, master's, and public
policy programmes.

Before graduate school I entered the civil service through IPDN, and my early
posts in North Sulawesi were in asset management and procurement: procurement
officer, then commitment-making official responsible for contracts, then member
of the provincial selection working group with authority over contracts up to
IDR 100 billion. From 2021 to 2023 I led the provincial sub-division responsible
for procurement advisory and technical guidance. Since 2018 I have worked
nationally as a certified procurement facilitator, and I now serve as a
competency assessor for the certification body of Indonesia's National Public
Procurement Agency, as a procurement advisor, and as a certified mediator under the
Supreme Court. I hold the World Bank's Certificate Professional in Public
Procurement.

That practical experience shaped what I find worth studying. Procurement is
where formal rules meet local discretion, and where the gap between what a
regulation requires and what an official can actually do is most visible. My
master's thesis used Indonesia's e-procurement records to ask whether more
bidders produce better outcomes, and was one of three theses at the faculty
selected for examination by the Minister of Finance.

The longer-term agenda is to keep both strands running: rigorous empirical
economics on shocks, institutions, and local public goods in Indonesia, and a
serious contribution to the professionalisation of Indonesian public
procurement, including writing about procurement practice for practitioners,
not only for regulators.
